newsitem.title: USA: Prepaid phone cards get better.
newsitem.headline: Prepaid phone cards get better.

text.p: If you are travelling a lot this summer and plan several long-distance check-ins with your family, boss, neighbours or voice mail message machine, you might want to invest in prepaid phone cards.
Those cards, blasted for their high rates when they first came on the scene a few years ago, have become more reasonably priced.

According to Consumer Action, a San Francisco organisation that monitors phone rates, regular long-distance fees have gone up about 25 percent over the last year, while rates on prepaid phone cards have dropped 20 percent.
"We even found prepaid cards that offer frequent flyer miles," said Consumer Action's Linda Sherry after the organisation's last survey.

With some prepaid phone cards charging as little as 14 cents per minute, they come very close to beating the lowest home-phone rates offered by the big three -- AT&T Corp., MCI Communications Corp. and Sprint Corp. When you are on the road, they look even better.

For example, AT&T's popular 15-cents-per-long-distance-minute plan only applies to calls from your home phone. Use your AT&T calling card from a pay phone and your rate doubles to 30 cents a minute. Even some of the more expensive prepaid cards beat that.
To get the most from a prepaid card, comparison shop for one that offers a good rate and is backed by a nationally known issuer.

Why? The bad news about these cards, according to Sherry, is this: Some of them offered such good rates that they went belly up, leaving customers with a card that was useless. Consumers who held cards backed by national issuers, such as the USA Calling Card issued by Kmart, received refunds.

Find out what the per-minute rate on your prepaid calling card is, and use it whenever it would be better than the regular rate you would otherwise get. On some plans, for example, you might decide to use your prepaid card during business hours but not on evenings or weekends. On others, your prepaid card might be better than anything else available while travelling.

That includes the old "charge-it-to-your-room" hotel rates. Be aware that even if you use a calling card, prepaid or otherwise, your hotel will probably mark up the call with a surcharge when you dial from your room. If it's not convenient to use a pay phone in the lobby, remember that you can often make more than one call on the same service charge if, instead of hanging up between calls, you press the "pound" key.
Finally, don't invest too much money in your first prepaid card. You might not like the service that comes with it.

Even if you do like it, you might find you don't use it as much as you thought you would, and most cards have expiration dates that run six months to a year from first use. Just put enough money on it to see if you like it and to learn your own calling pattern.
Some cards are rechargeable from the road. You can call an 800 number and get more money put into your account with a credit card number.
To get a complete list of prepaid cards and their current rates and rules, send a stamped, self-addressed envelope to Consumer Action, 116 New Monthgomery Street, Suite 233, San Francisco, CA 94105.

You can e-mail Linda Stern at 72160.1546(at)compuserve.com or write to her in care of Reuters, Suite 410, 1333 H St., NW, Washington, DC 20005. She regrets that she cannot answer each letter individually but will cover your questions in upcoming columns.
(EDITORS: Linda Stern is a free-lance writer who covers personal finance issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Ms. Stern.)
